anatomy.lede: Long, eel-like and dark brown, the frilled shark has a head unlike any other living shark: a mouth at the very tip of the snout and gills edged with frills.

hotspots.label: Snout-tip mouth
hotspots.text: Unlike most sharks, whose mouths sit underneath the head, the frilled shark's mouth is at the front of the snout.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: The eyes are moderately large horizontal ovals and have no protective third eyelid.

hotspots.label: Three-pronged teeth
hotspots.text: About 300 trident-shaped teeth line the jaws in 19–29 rows. The small, sharp teeth point inwards.

hotspots.label: Long jaws
hotspots.text: The jaws hinge directly to the skull behind the eyes. This is thought to give it a relatively weak bite.

hotspots.label: Frilled gills
hotspots.text: There are six gill slits on each side, not the usual five, and their frilly edges give the shark its name.

senses.lede: How a frilled shark finds food in the dark is mostly inferred from its anatomy.

senses.name: Open lateral line
senses.text: Its lateral line is an open groove, with sensory hair cells exposed directly to the water, which helps it sense movement, vibration and pressure.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: The eyes are moderately large, but how well it sees has not been studied.

body.lede: Many features of the frilled shark look like those of very early sharks.

systems.title: A simple backbone
systems.text: The skeleton is cartilage, and the spinal column is a notochord with only poorly defined vertebrae.

systems.title: An oily liver
systems.text: A large liver full of oil helps it control its buoyancy.

systems.title: Slow digestion?
systems.text: Of 139 sharks examined from Suruga Bay, Japan, 73% had empty stomachs, an unusually high share for a deep-water shark, and the food that was found was heavily digested.

mind.lede: Almost nothing has been watched directly; its hunting style is pieced together from stomachs, captives and its body shape.

studies.title: A squid specialist
studies.text: Squid and other cephalopods were found in 60% of stomachs that held food, and fish in about 10%. Beaks showed it eats both deep-water and near-surface squid.

studies.title: Strike like a snake
studies.text: It may bend its body, brace with its rear fins and lunge forward to seize prey, like a striking snake.

studies.title: A gleaming lure
studies.text: Captive frilled sharks have been seen swimming with their mouths open. Their white teeth against the dark mouth may attract prey.

survival.lede: A slow-breeding shark is easily harmed by even modest fishing.

tactics.title: Living deep
tactics.text: It usually stays between 500 and 1,000 m, on outer shelves, slopes and seamounts.

threats.title: Bycatch
threats.text: It is not targeted, but is caught by accident in deep-water bottom trawls and other fishing gear, and sometimes used for fishmeal or food.

threats.title: Very slow to recover
threats.text: With few young and a very long pregnancy, its population is estimated to take more than 14 years to double.

life.lede: The frilled shark breeds extremely slowly, carrying its young for years.

stages.name: Egg capsule
stages.text: Eggs develop inside the mother in capsules, which are shed when the embryos reach 6–8 cm. Early development is slow.

stages.name: Embryo
stages.text: The embryos live on yolk inside the uterus. Based on 264 sharks from Suruga Bay, Japan, gestation was estimated at three and a half years or more.

stages.name: Birth
stages.text: Pups are born at about 55 cm long and 380 g, in litters of 2–10, with an average of six.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Males mature below about 1.1 m long and females at 1.4–1.5 m. Females have no fixed breeding season.
